About the Team

Hi! 🚀 We are two Computer Science students at Politehnica University of Timișoara, Romania, with an interest in software development, AI, cloud technologies, and space exploration.

About the Challenge

For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a large collection of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand.

Based on our initial research into NASA's experiments and available scientific data, we are developing MissionGuard — an AI-assisted, interactive dashboard designed to bring these findings together, make them easier to explore, and help identify meaningful patterns and fire safety insights.
summary:
MissionGuard is a spacecraft monitoring dashboard powered by AI technology created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The platform is dedicated to increasing spacecraft safety through monitoring telemetry, identifying any abnormalities, analyzing their root cause, and simulating spacecraft malfunction.

The platform integrates interactive visualizations of telemetry with anomaly detection approaches, namely threshold-based detection, rolling z-score analysis, and rate-of-change monitoring. The MissionGuard AI Mission Assistant will assist users in analyzing unusual telemetry readings, suggesting a root cause and offering recommendations, separating hypotheses and conclusions.

Also, the platform has a scenario simulator that will let users explore various spacecraft malfunction scenarios, including overheating batteries, solar panels deterioration, communication signals losing, and unexpected rotation.

Through converting telemetry into actionable safety information, the MissionGuard seeks to help with monitoring, investigation, and decision making related to future human space missions.
details:
Project Details – MissionGuard

MissionGuard is an AI-assisted microgravity fire-safety and spacecraft telemetry monitoring platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge "Flame in Freefall".

The application combines two distinct data domains, which are explicitly separated throughout the platform:

1. Real NASA Experimental Data – PSI-100 / SAFFIRE-III

MissionGuard integrates real NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) experimental telemetry from the Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III). Through NASA's PSI repository and API, the platform retrieves experimental combustion measurements, including radiometric heat flux, igniter-current pulses, duct airflow, fan speed, and Cygnus module smoke, temperature, and pressure measurements.

The application provides interactive visualizations, telemetry analysis, anomaly detection, and AI-assisted explanations of combustion-related events.

2. Synthetic Spacecraft Telemetry – AURA-SAT-4

A separate spacecraft monitoring module uses a deterministic, simulated 24-hour Low Earth Orbit telemetry dataset. It demonstrates subsystem monitoring, anomaly detection, and hypothetical spacecraft fault scenarios, including battery overheating, solar panel degradation, communication loss, and unexpected spacecraft rotation. These measurements are synthetic and are not presented as real NASA spacecraft telemetry.

Anomaly Detection and AI Assistance

The platform uses engineering thresholds, rolling Z-score analysis, and rate-of-change detection to identify unusual telemetry behavior.

The AI Mission Assistant uses Google Gemini to generate diagnostic explanations and potential engineering hypotheses, with a local rule-based fallback when an API key is unavailable. AI-generated explanations are intended as hypotheses, not confirmed root causes.

Technology Stack

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Node.js, Express, Recharts, Lucide React, and the Google Gemini API.

AI-assisted development tools, including Google AI Studio and Gemini, were used for portions of the application development, code generation, and troubleshooting.

MissionGuard aims to make microgravity combustion measurements more accessible and interpretable while demonstrating how intelligent monitoring could contribute to fire-safety research for future human space exploration.

The project is an educational and research prototype, not a certified operational spacecraft safety system.
